claims.sentence: The NHS lists trapped wind, indigestion, constipation and a stomach bug or food poisoning as common everyday causes of stomach ache.
claims.evidence: NHS stomach ache table: bloated/farting a lot -> trapped wind; full after eating, heartburn -> indigestion; hard to poo -> constipation; watery poo, sick -> stomach bug or food poisoning.

claims.sentence: Period pain and endometriosis are listed as causes of pain in the lower tummy in women.
claims.evidence: Retrieved text links intense pain around the time of a period (with possible pain during/after sex and when pooing) to endometriosis. Plain 'period pain' as a listed cause, and 'lower tummy in women', were not seen.
claims.newSentence: The NHS links intense pain around the time of a period, sometimes with pain during or after sex and when pooing, with endometriosis.

claims.sentence: The NHS stomach ache page links pain in the lower right side of the tummy with appendicitis.
claims.evidence: NHS stomach ache page: right lower abdominal pain can indicate appendicitis.

claims.sentence: It links severe pain that lasts up to 8 hours in the centre of the tummy, or just under the ribs on the right, with gallstones.
claims.evidence: NHS 111 Wales lists gallstones for severe pain lasting hours in the upper centre of the tummy or under the right ribs. nhs.uk gallstones says pain usually lasts 1 to 5 hours; 8 hours is a GP-contact threshold, not a duration of the pain. Attribution to the NHS stomach ache page not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: NHS 111 Wales links severe pain that lasts for hours in the upper centre of the tummy, or just under the ribs on the right, with gallstones.

claims.sentence: It links ongoing cramps, bloating, diarrhoea and constipation with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
claims.evidence: NHS stomach ache page: ongoing cramps, bloating and changed bowel habits suggest IBS.

claims.sentence: NHS inform describes appendicitis as painful swelling of the appendix, and says the pain of IBS is often relieved by going to the toilet.
claims.evidence: NHS inform: appendicitis is painful swelling of the appendix (supported). For IBS it says pain and cramping 'may be relieved by moving your bowels'; 'often' overstates.
claims.newSentence: NHS inform describes appendicitis as painful swelling of the appendix, and says the pain and cramping of IBS may be relieved by going to the toilet.

claims.sentence: Stomach ulcer pain is usually in the upper tummy, may feel burning and is often worse at night.
claims.evidence: NHS: stomach ulcer pain is usually felt in the upper tummy, may feel like burning and is often worse at night.

claims.sentence: Gastritis can cause pain, indigestion and feeling sick.
claims.evidence: NHS gastritis: can cause pain, indigestion and feeling sick.

claims.sentence: Gastritis is inflammation of the lining of the stomach.
claims.evidence: NHS: gastritis is when the lining of the stomach becomes irritated (inflamed). Author marked textbook; retrieved text also says it.

claims.sentence: Acute pancreatitis causes severe pain that develops suddenly in the centre of the tummy, and the NHS says its most common causes are gallstones and drinking a lot of alcohol.
claims.evidence: NHS: severe dull pain around the top of the stomach that develops suddenly (upper abdomen), not the centre generally; gallstones about half and alcohol about a quarter of cases.
claims.newSentence: Acute pancreatitis causes severe pain around the top of the tummy that develops suddenly, and gallstones and alcohol are its most common causes.

claims.sentence: Appendicitis is when the appendix becomes inflamed; it usually causes pain in the lower right side of the tummy and is sometimes accompanied by nausea and loss of appetite.
claims.evidence: NHS 111 Wales: swelling and infection of the appendix, usually pain in the lower right of the abdomen; associated nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite.

claims.sentence: An NHS 111 Wales page says appendicitis needs urgent treatment in hospital.
claims.evidence: NHS 111 Wales: appendicitis needs urgent treatment in hospital.

claims.sentence: A hospital trust page says gallstones do not always cause symptoms, but can lead to pain after eating, inflammation of the gallbladder, pancreatitis or jaundice.
claims.evidence: The Chesterfield (cht.nhs.uk) page did not come back. NHS gallstones results say most people with gallstones never get symptoms, and a stone can cause pain, jaundice (blocked bile duct) or pancreatitis (blocked pancreatic duct).
claims.newSentence: Many people with gallstones have no symptoms, but a stone can cause pain, jaundice or pancreatitis.

claims.sentence: The NHS says diverticular disease causes pain in the lower left side of the tummy that often gets worse after eating and eases after passing wind or stool, with constipation, diarrhoea, bloating or blood in the stool.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: lower left-sided pain; NHS inform says diverticulitis is more serious, with more severe pain especially on the left, fever of 38C or above, diarrhoea. Worse after eating / eases after wind or stool and the symptom list were not seen; nhs.uk page itself did not return.
claims.newSentence: NHS inform says diverticulitis, the inflamed form of diverticular disease, tends to cause more severe tummy pain, especially on the left side, and a fever of 38C or above.

claims.sentence: It adds that the symptoms are similar to those of other conditions such as IBS.
claims.evidence: Not found in retrieved text.

claims.sentence: For diverticular disease the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for blood in the stool, worsening or persistent tummy pain, or a fever, and says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, being unable to pass stool or wind, or signs of sepsis.
claims.evidence: Only NHS 111 Wales text retrieved: urgent GP or 111 for blood or mucus in stool, pain that worsens or will not go away, high temperature or shivers, persistent vomiting. The 999/A&E list in the sentence was not confirmed; snippets cut off before it. Route to care and publisher not matched.
claims.newSentence: NHS 111 Wales advises urgent help from a GP or NHS 111 for blood or mucus in the stool, pain that gets worse or does not go away, or a high temperature or shivers.

claims.sentence: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if the pain started suddenly and is severe.
claims.evidence: NHS stomach ache page: call 999 or go to A&E if the pain started suddenly and is severe.

claims.sentence: Other reasons are vomiting blood or vomit that looks green or like ground coffee, a lot of blood from the bottom or black, sticky poo, being unable to pee at all, being unable to poo or fart at all, a rash that does not fade when pressed, or struggling to breathe.
claims.evidence: Stomach ache page retrieval confirmed: confusion, difficulty breathing, blue/grey/pale/blotchy skin, lips or tongue. Bright red or coffee-ground vomit and blood/black sticky poo appear on the stomach ulcer page, not confirmed for the stomach ache page. Green vomit, unable to pee, unable to poo or fart, and non-blanching rash were not seen.
claims.newSentence: Other reasons on the NHS page include struggling to breathe, confusion, and blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin, lips or tongue.

claims.sentence: NHS inform adds chest pain, and pain that hurts when the stomach is touched, to the reasons to call 999.
claims.evidence: NHS inform: call 999 for stomach ache that came on very suddenly or is severe, plus chest pain and difficulty breathing. Pain on touching the stomach not seen.
claims.newSentence: NHS inform adds chest pain and difficulty breathing to the reasons to call 999.

claims.sentence: For acute pancreatitis, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if the pain spreads to the back, or if there is a fast heartbeat or difficulty breathing.
claims.evidence: NHS: call 999 or go to A&E if you have sudden, severe tummy pain AND any of: pain spreading to the back, bloating that will not go away, fast heartbeat or difficulty breathing, bluish/bruised skin around the belly button, waist or upper outer thigh. The sentence drops the sudden-severe condition and implies each alone is enough.
claims.newSentence: For acute pancreatitis, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden, severe tummy pain together with any of: pain spreading to the back, bloating that does not go away, a fast heartbeat or difficulty breathing.

claims.sentence: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if the ache suddenly gets much worse, if the person is pregnant, if there is blood in the poo, or if diarrhoea or vomiting has lasted several days.
claims.evidence: NHS stomach ache page: ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if it suddenly gets much worse, you are pregnant, blood in your poo; diarrhoea or vomiting that persists several days.

claims.sentence: It advises a GP appointment for pain, bloating or indigestion that does not go away or keeps coming back, for a lump in the tummy, or for losing weight without trying.
claims.evidence: Not seen in any retrieved text this session (search budget exhausted before a targeted re-check; could be re-verified).

claims.sentence: Treatment depends on the cause.
claims.evidence: NHS stomach ulcer treatment: depends on the cause; same principle on stomach ache pages.

claims.sentence: For gastritis, a GP might arrange a breath test for Helicobacter pylori bacteria, a stool test or a blood test.
claims.evidence: NHS: tests for H. pylori are a urea breath test, stool antigen test and blood test (result blended from gastritis/ulcer pages).

claims.sentence: Stomach ulcers may be treated with antibiotics for a Helicobacter pylori infection or with medicines that reduce stomach acid, such as proton pump inhibitors.
claims.evidence: NHS: H. pylori ulcers get antibiotics plus a PPI; NSAID-caused ulcers get a PPI; PPIs reduce stomach acid.

claims.sentence: Gastroenteritis often has no specific treatment, and the illness has to run its course.
claims.evidence: No NHS inform or NHS gastroenteritis text came back.

claims.sentence: Where a stomach ache sits helps point to causes such as appendicitis, gallstones or IBS, and sudden severe pain needs 999 or A&E.
claims.evidence: NHS stomach ache page maps location/symptoms to appendicitis, gallstones, IBS and says call 999 or go to A&E for sudden severe pain. Keep consistent with edited gallstone sentence.
